plans.objective: [DIM: optimization] The minimal width $N_c(w)$ required for zero violation exhibits a phase transition at a critical constraint density $\rho_c \approx w/H$, where below $\rho_c$, the optimization landscape is benign and $N_c(w)$ remains bounded, while above $\rho_c$, the problem becomes over-parameterized and $N_c(w)$ grows indefinitely, indicating a shift from rigid to fat solution spaces. This hypothesis is the most testable and novel because it directly addresses the core question of how network capacity relates to constraint satisfaction and can be validated through straightforward numerical experiments. The phase transition provides a clear and interpretable result, making it easier to draw meaningful conclusions about the rigidity of the solution space.

steps.description: Design and implement a numerical experiment to test the phase transition hypothesis in the minimal width N_c(w) for zero-violation constraint satisfaction. The experiment will: (1) define a constraint satisfaction problem with w constraints, (2) vary hidden layer width N to find the minimum N_c(w) achieving zero violation (max absolute error ≤ 1e-3 on held-out constraints), (3) scan constraint density ρ = w/H to identify the critical point ρ_c ≈ w/H where N_c(w) transitions from bounded to divergent. Implementation will use small feedforward networks with standard activation functions, and will include convergence checks, validation splits, and repeated trials for statistical robustness. The code will be written in Python with PyTorch, ensuring reproducibility and adherence to the zero-violation criterion.

plans.objective: [DIM: structure] The minimal width $N_c(w)$ is determined by the algebraic rank of the constraint matrix formed by the network's feature activations at the training points; specifically, $N_c(w) \ge w$ for exact interpolation, but due to ReLU piecewise linearity, $N_c(w)$ saturates at a constant threshold when the network can represent the piecewise linear interpolant with fewer than $w$ active regions.

[DIM: structure] The zero-violation capacity $N_c(w)$ is determined by the algebraic rank of the Jacobian matrix of the network outputs with respect to the weights at the constraint points; specifically, rigid behavior occurs when the rank of this matrix reaches $w$, implying that $N_c(w)$ is governed by the structural ability of the ReLU network to span the constraint space, rather than just optimization difficulty.

[DIM: structure] The zero-violation capacity $N_c(w)$ is determined by the algebraic rank of the Jacobian matrix of the network's feature map at the constraint points; specifically, $N_c(w) = \lceil w / d_{\text{eff}} \rceil$ where $d_{\text{eff}}$ is the effective dimension of the ReLU activation subspace spanned by the hidden units.

steps.description: We will test the hypothesis that zero-violation capacity $N_c(w) = \lceil w / d_{\text{eff}} \rceil$ by designing a numerical experiment on small ReLU networks. We will: (1) generate a family of analytic constraint functions (e.g., polynomials, sinusoids) to serve as target functions; (2) for each target, sweep constraint counts $w \in \{5, 10, 15, \dots, 30\}$ and hidden widths $N \in \{5, 10, \dots, 50\}$; (3) train networks to satisfy constraints with max absolute error $\le 1e-3$ on held-out points; (4) record the minimal $N$ achieving zero violation for each $w$; (5) compute effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}$ via Jacobian rank at constraint points and compare against observed $N_c(w)$. This is a direct test of the algebraic rank hypothesis.

plans.objective: [DIM: optimization] The minimal width $N_c(w)$ required for zero-violation generalization exhibits a sharp phase transition at a critical constraint density $\rho_c = w/N$, below which the loss landscape contains a connected basin of global minima and above which it becomes disconnected, causing $N_c(w)$ to diverge.

steps.description: We will test the hypothesis that zero-violation capacity $N_c(w)$ exhibits a phase transition at critical constraint density $\rho_c = w/N$ by designing a rigorous numerical experiment on small ReLU networks. Specifically: (1) define the constraint function as a system of linear equations $Wx = b$ (where $W \in \mathbb{R}^{w \times N}$ is the weight matrix and $x \in \mathbb{R}^N$ is the input) to ensure exact zero-violation satisfaction; (2) generate input data samples from a standard normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(0, I_N)$ to compute $\rho$; (3) use a single-layer ReLU network with Xavier initialization to control depth and activation effects; (4) measure basin connectivity via geodesic path finding in weight space between randomly initialized global minima (verified by near-zero loss); and (5) scan width $N \in [10, 100]$ and constraint count $w \in [1, 200]$ with step sizes $\Delta N=5, \Delta w=2$ to identify the transition point where $N_c(w)$ diverges.

plans.objective: [DIM: structure] The minimal width $N_c(w)$ for zero-violation generalization is determined by the algebraic rank of the constraint matrix $A_{ij} = \phi_j(x_i)$ formed by the network's basis functions evaluated at constraint points; $N_c(w) \ge \text{rank}(A)$, and rigidity occurs when $\text{rank}(A) = w$ for $N \ll w$.

steps.description: We will test the hypothesis that zero-violation capacity $N_c(w)$ is determined by the algebraic rank of the constraint matrix $A_{ij} = \phi_j(x_i)$ by designing a numerical experiment on small fully-connected ReLU networks. We will: (1) generate constraint points $x_i$ on a 1D interval using an adaptive grid; (2) define basis functions $\phi_j(x)$ as the pre-activation outputs of the first hidden layer; (3) compute the rank of $A$ analytically and numerically; (4) train networks of increasing width $w$ to minimize $\max |f(x_i) - y_i|$; (5) identify the minimum width $N_c(w)$ achieving zero violation ($\le 1e-3$); and (6) verify if rigidity occurs when rank(A) approaches $w$ for $N \ll w$.
